name: Arkansas

agency.name: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, Labor Standards Division

minWage.smallEmployer: The Arkansas Minimum Wage Act covers employers with 4 or more employees; smaller employers are subject only to the federal FLSA ($7.25) if covered by it.

tipped.note: tips must bring the employee up to $11.00; employer makes up any shortfall

minWage.other: Employers may apply to the Labor Standards Division for a reduced minimum wage for students (application form on the agency page).

source.quote: Effective January 1, 2021, the minimum wage in Arkansas is $11.00 per hour. The Arkansas Minimum Wage Act covers employers with 4 or more employees.

overtime.exemptSalaryNote: no state salary level above the federal $684/week
overtime.note: time and a half after 40 hours actually worked in a workweek; no daily overtime

source.quote: an employer has to pay overtime (one and one-half times the regular rate of pay) to non-exempt employees for all hours actually worked in excess of 40 hours in a workweek

sickLeave.note: No state paid sick leave law for private employers; sick pay is owed only if company policy provides it.

source.quote: If you are filing a wage claim because you believe you are due vacation pay, sick pay, holiday pay ... you must provide us a copy of the company policy
The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides certain employees with up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave per year

finalPay.fired: by the next regular payday (if not paid within 7 days of that payday, the employer owes double the wages due)
finalPay.ptoNote: vacation pay is owed at separation only if the company policy provides it

source.quote: If a company or corporation terminates the employee, the employee's wages are due by the next regular payday. If the employer fails to make payment within 7 days of the next regular payday then the employer shall owe the employee double the wages due.

ptoSource.quote: If you are filing a wage claim because you believe you are due vacation pay ... you must provide us a copy of the company policy that states you will be paid

breaks.minorsOnly: Rest breaks are required only for children under 16 employed in the entertainment industry.

source.quote: Neither state nor federal wage and hour laws require an employer to provide a break or a meal period. (State law does require rest breaks for children under the age of 16 employed in the entertainment industry.)

notes.text: The state minimum wage law applies only to employers with 4 or more employees; when both state and federal law apply, the higher rate ($11.00) must be paid.

source.quote: Employers covered by the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) are also covered by the Arkansas law if they have 4 or more employees. An employer covered by both laws must pay the highest minimum wage.

notes.text: An employer that pays final wages more than 7 days after the next regular payday owes the worker double the wages due.

source.quote: If the employer fails to make payment within 7 days of the next regular payday then the employer shall owe the employee double the wages due.

notes.text: The Labor Standards Division handles wage claims of $2,000 or less, and only for workers earning $50,000 a year or less; larger claims go to court (Small Claims Court possible without an attorney).

source.quote: You are not eligible to file a wage claim if : *the amount in dispute is more than $2000; or *you make more than $50,000 per year.

uncertain: rightToWork: Arkansas is generally known as a right-to-work state (Constitution Amendment 34), but the official constitution/statute text could not be retrieved today (SOS PDF link broken, legislature/Lexis code portal not fetchable, WebSearch quota exhausted). Set to null pending verification.

finalPay.quit: the official FAQ only addresses employees terminated by the employer (next regular payday); no official page read today states the rule for employees who quit. Ark. Code 11-4-405 text not retrievable.

rates2027: no official announcement of a 2027 change found on the agency page (rate unchanged since 2021); no indexed statute adjustment exists to my knowledge, but no official 2027 statement was read.
